title: Q&A: Noam Lupu on How Latin Americans View Democracy
gist: Noam Lupu of LAPOP says the latest AmericasBarometer (first to include Cuba) shows regional optimism about economies, security and democracy rebounding from a low baseline, while trust in the U.S. government has fallen below trust in China. He warns the uptick reflects transactional views of democracy.

insights.claim: The latest AmericasBarometer found Latin Americans more positive than three years ago about their personal circumstances, the economy, security, democracy and political institutions.
insights.speaker: EMILIE SWEIGART
insights.so_what: Improving sentiment suggests tailwinds for incumbents elected on change platforms, but from a depressed baseline.

insights.claim: The sentiment improvement is attributed to receding post-pandemic inflation and heavy government turnover that raised hope that new governments will do things differently.
insights.speaker: EMILIE SWEIGART
insights.so_what: Optimism is tied to honeymoon effects and disinflation, so it can fade if delivery disappoints.

insights.claim: The uptick is described as coming off a pretty low baseline; people in the region still struggle and remain dissatisfied with their political systems, following declines since the end of the commodity boom.
insights.speaker: EMILIE SWEIGART
insights.so_what: Do not over-read the rebound as structural improvement in political stability.
insights.quote: It’s an uptick from a pretty low baseline, and in general, people are still having a hard time and are still not satisfied with their political systems.

insights.claim: Perceptions of the U.S. government have become much more negative across Latin America over three years, with trust in the U.S. declining since 2021.
insights.speaker: EMILIE SWEIGART
insights.so_what: Falling U.S. soft power in the region raises odds of hedging toward other partners.
insights.locator: attitudes toward the United States and China

insights.claim: Trust in China fell during the pandemic but has recovered to pre-pandemic levels, so China is now seen as a more trustworthy partner than the U.S. government in the region.
insights.speaker: EMILIE SWEIGART
insights.so_what: Supports a thesis of expanding Chinese commercial and diplomatic room in Latin America.
insights.quote: China is now seen as a more trustworthy partner than the U.S. government.
insights.locator: attitudes toward the United States and China

insights.claim: Lupu worries that support for democracy that rests on economic and security delivery is a thin basis for commitment, and that a transactional view of political systems threatens long-term democratic sustainability.
insights.speaker: EMILIE SWEIGART
insights.so_what: Democratic support could reverse quickly if growth or security deteriorates, raising political risk and strongman appeal.
insights.quote: If democracy to folks in the region is only good when it delivers economic benefits and reduced crime, that’s a thin basis for commitment to democracy.

insights.claim: The survey covered Cuba for the first time, coinciding with changing U.S. policy toward Cuba, to capture everyday Cubans' views that observers usually omit.
insights.speaker: EMILIE SWEIGART
insights.so_what: New Cuba opinion data is a gauge of public mood as U.S.-Cuba policy shifts.
